content.title: Response to Reviewer zPyW (1/2)
content.comment:
- **Q1. Given the closeness between the proposal and VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN, I don't understand why those baseline are not in Table 1.**

    Indeed, VQ-LSTM (one of the baselines) is based on VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN. Note that VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN are for image data and so cannot be applied directly on time series data. Hence, in VQ-LSTM, we changed the Stage I autoencoder in VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN to one with 1D-convolution (as in the proposed method). As for the Stage II predictor, VQ-VAE uses a PixelCNN while VQ-GAN uses a transformer. However, PixelCNN is for two-dimensional data and not for sequential data. Moreover, the ablation study in Section 4.2.3 and [1] suggest that the transformer may not be suitable for time series data. Hence, we changed the Stage II predictor to a LSTM in VQ-LSTM.

- **Q2. What is the gain associated with the GAN Loss and the memory (wrt VQ-VAE)**

    The gain associated with the memory can be observed by comparing MATS and VQ-LSTM. as discussed in the reply above, VQ-LSTM is based on VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN and uses a discrete codebook, without using continuous memory bank as in MATS.

    As for the gain associated with the GAN loss, we now add in Appendix A.4 an ablation study that removes the GAN loss (i.e., discriminator) from stage I. Table 1 below shows the effect of removing the discriminator from Stage I of MATS. As in Table 3 of the original submission, we also use the Electricity and Exchange datasets. Moreover, as suggested by the reviewer, here we experiment with both the univariate and multivariate versions of the time series data. We set $T/T' = 12$ as in the other experiments. As can be seen, the discriminator (GAN loss) can improve the performance of MATS in many cases, especially in long-term prediction ($H = 720$) on the more difficult dataset (`Electricity`).

    *Table 1: MSE with or without discriminator on `Electricity` and `Exchange`.*
    | |H|Univariate Electricity|Univariate Exchange|Multivariate Electricity|Multivariate Exchange
    |:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|

content.title: Response to Reviewer zPyW (2/2)
content.comment:
- **Q3. Fig. 2 results seem quite unrealistic. It is logical to select samples with good performances... But we really wonder how the model can be so accurate given the first part of the signal. It would have been interesting to have the whole explanation in appendix (memory usage & corresponding patterns).**

    Indeed, the sample shown in Figure 2 is simply the first testing sample, and thus is not carefully selected. We now add more samples (which are picked every 160 samples) to Appendix B.1.

    As on why the model works so well, we add in Appendix B.2 an illustration and analysis with a synthetic univariate time series: $x_t = \sin(0.08(t-1) + \pi/2) + 0.6\sin(0.2(t-1) + \pi)$, where $t = 1,\dots,10240$. To reduce the redundancy of the memory units, the memory size $M$ is set to 4.
    The training set $\mathcal{X}$ has $N$ length-96 time series segments. After Stage I training, we compute the average memory attention value as follows. Each of the $N$ training time series $\mathbf{x}$ is fed through the encoder and memory bank to obtain $\{\mathcal{M} \circ \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\}\_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}$, where each $\mathcal{M} \circ \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\in [0,1]^{M\times T'}$ (and $T' = 8$). This is then averaged over the time dimension to obtain $\bar{\mathbf{c}}=[\bar{c}\_1, \bar{c}\_2, \dots, \bar{c}\_M] \in[0, 1]^M$, where $\bar{c}\_i = \frac{2}{NT'} \sum\_{t=1}^{T'}\sum\_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{[\mathcal{M} \circ \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})]\_{t,i}}$.

    We then compute the average memory attention for each memory unit $i$ as $\mathbf{C}^i=[\mathbf{c}^i_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}^i_{T'}] \in [0,1]^{M\times T'}$, $c^i\_{t,i} = \bar{c}\_i$ and $c^i\_{t, j} = 0$ for $j\ne i$. This is then fed to decoder $\mathcal{D}$ (using Equation (2)). The decoder outputs are shown in Figure 7(a) in this updated version. As can be seen, they all represent different local patterns.

    To further study how the memory units jointly represent the time series, we feed in the first training sample and obtain the memory attention sequence $\mathbf{C}=[\mathbf{c}\_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}\_{T'}] \in [0,1]^{M\times T'}$ using Equation (1). For each column vector $\mathbf{c}_{t}\in [0, 1]^M$ of $\mathbf{C}$ (i.e. the memory attention), we keep only its top-$k$ values, and set the remaining entries to zero. Let the resultant memory attention matrix be $\mathbf{C}^{(k)}=[\mathbf{c}^{(k)}\_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}^{(k)}\_{T'}]$. Setting $k = 1,2,3,4$, we then feed them into the decoder and obtain the top1, top2, top3, top4 outputs using Equation (2). Results are shown in Figure 7(b) in this updated version. We can observe that i) the top1 curve is around the mean of the time series; ii) the top2 curve has similar shape to the ground truth (i.e., the input time series), which implies that using two memory units can already roughly represent its shape; iii) the top3 and top4 curves are even more refined, providing more details of the time series.


[1] A. Zeng, M. Chen, L. Zhang, and Q. Xu, "Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?," Preprint arXiv:2205.13504, 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a solution from long-term time-series forecasting, which is a key application for ML. Their model is based on a memory bank that uses an autoencoder to extract and store short-term temporal patterns in the input. The patterns stored in the memory bank essentially chunk the input sequence into a smaller number of tokens. An attention mechanism then retrieves patterns from the memory bank to represent the current input. These reweighted representations are called "memory attentions", also $C$. The input memory attentions are fed into a predictor which outputs new memory attentions $\hat{C}$, which correspond to predictions of the next H steps in the sequence. All memory attention representations are fed to a decoder which maps $C$ and $\hat{C}$ back to the original time domain. Together they call this the "Memory Attention for Time Series" model (MATS). The authors then conduct extensive comparisons to existing models for time-series forecasting, illustrating that they beat the SOTA much of the time. They also add some experiments to understand how the performance of the model varies when changing key hyperparameters or portions of the model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- Well-motivated work on a problem that is in need of further advances
- Good related work section
- Clear explanation of model with all the necessary technical details
- Extensive experimental comparisons with many related/competing models
- Beats SOTA much of the time, even with a variant of the model (VQ-LSTM) which uses a codebook instead of a memory bank

Weaknesses
- "Ablation" studies mostly just vary some parameter, rather than being a true ablation experiment which removes an element completely from a model
    - Furthermore, these experiments were limited (e.g. only evaluating on univariate datasets) and do not give much insight into the workings of the model. They seem somewhat preliminary.
    - e.g. when varying the size of the memory bank -- there seems to be no improvement after a given size. Is it possible to determine the memory size analytically somehow, based on the statistics of the dataset? Seeing the same analysis on other datasets would be useful to answer this question.

Further questions/clarifications
- Please add detail on whether you used existing implementations of the competing models shown in Tables 1 & 2, or implemented your own version.
- Why did you set $T/T' = 12$ for all datasets? From Table 3 it seems that the best performance comes from $T/T' = 24$.
- The transformer vs. LSTM experimental results were a bit surprising to me. The paper is missing details to allow me to really evaluate this -- e.g. what are the relative sizes of the two architectures (e.g. number of transformer heads, layers, etc.). It is also possible that the complexity of a multivariate dataset would allow the transformer to perform better than the LSTM.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: the paper was clear and contained the details needed to evaluate the results.

Quality: no issues or concerns with quality of the implementation or experiments. The claims made in the paper are supported by the data.

Novelty: the proposal is sensible and novel, to my knowledge. It takes advantage of some ideas on chunking sequences into shorter patterns to build an effective forecasting model. I am familiar with some of the slightly older literature on this topic (>= 2 years ago) so I feel fairly confident in this assessment.

Reproducibility: Links to all the datasets are provided. While the authors do not share their code (from what I could see), it does not appear to be missing key details that would be needed to reproduce the results (although see "Further questions/clarifications" above).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the novelty, clarity, and quality of the proposal and experiments lead me to recommend accepting this paper. While I would typically have rated this paper a 7, it does not seem like this is a choice available to me -- therefore I'm rating it an 8, because it exceeds the bar for a marginal acceptance.

content.title: Response to Reviewer V16Y (1/3)
content.comment:
- **Q1. "Ablation" studies mostly just vary some parameter, rather than being a true ablation experiment which removes an element completely from a model. ... only evaluating on univariate datasets**

    In the submitted version, the VQ-LSTM baseline replaces the continuous memory bank MATS with a discrete codebook (as in VQ-VAE/VQ-GAN). Moreover, preliminary results in Table 3 of the original submission also show the effect of removing time dimension compression (i.e., setting $T' = T = 96$). As suggested by this reviewer and also reviewer zPyW, we now add some more ablation studies, which are now added (in blue) in Sections 4.2.2-4.2.3 and Section A.4 of this revised version.

    First, Table 1 below shows the effect of removing the discriminator from Stage I of MATS. As in Table 3 of the original submission, we also use the Electricity and Exchange datasets. Moreover, as suggested by the reviewer, here we experiment with both the univariate and multivariate versions of the time series data. We set $T/T' = 12$ as in the other experiments. As can be seen, the discriminator (GAN loss) can improve the performance of MATS in many cases, especially in long-term prediction ($H = 720$) on the more difficult dataset (`Electricity`).

    *Table 1: MSE with or without discriminator on `Electricity` and `Exchange`.*
    | |H|Univariate Electricity|Univariate Exchange|Multivariate Electricity|Multivariate Exchange
    |:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
    |With discriminator|96|**0.177**|**0.019**|**0.156**|**0.034**|
    |With discriminator|192|0.252|**0.044**|**0.165**|0.049|
    |With discriminator|336|**0.260**|**0.069**|**0.168**|**0.073**|
    |With discriminator|720|**0.286**|0.262|**0.179**|0.135|
    |Without discriminator|96|0.185|**0.019**|0.158|0.034|
    |Without discriminator|192|**0.243**|0.045|**0.165**|0.048|
    |Without discriminator|336|0.277|0.075|0.169|**0.073**|
    |Without discriminator|720|0.311|**0.219**|0.183|**0.126**|

    We also expand the ablation study on the effect of time dimension compression (Table 3 in the original submission). We use $T = 96$, $H = 96$, and vary $T'$ from 2 to 96. In this revised version, we add the multivariate versions of the datasets. Results are shown in Table 2 below. As can be seen, performance on both the univariate and multivariate datasets degrade when time dimension compression is not used (i.e., $T' = T = 96$).

    Moreover, while a smaller $T'$ ($T' = 4$) performs better on the univariate datasets, a bigger $T'$ is better ($T' = 32$) on the multivariate datasets. This is because when $T'$ is too small, the short attention sequence may not be able to represent the complex pattern in a multivariate time series.

    *Table 2: MSE with $T'$ on the `Electricity` and `Exchange` (with $T = 96$, $H = 96$).*

It may be because transformers are more appropriate when the input sequence is long, while here, we have compressed the input time series to shorter attention sequences of length T′ + H′. Also, [1] argues that transformers may not be suitable for time series forecasting.

content.title: Response to Reviewer V16Y (2/3)
content.comment:
- **Q2. do not give much insight into the workings of the model**

    As suggested, we first add in Appendix B.2 an illustration with a synthetic univariate time series: $x_t = \sin(0.08(t-1) + \pi/2) + 0.6\sin(0.2(t-1) + \pi)$, where $t = 1,\dots,10240$. To reduce the redundancy of the memory units, the memory size $M$ is set to 4.
    The training set $\mathcal{X}$ has $N$ length-96 time series segments. After Stage I training, we compute the average memory attention value as follows. Each of the $N$ training time series $\mathbf{x}$ is fed through the encoder and memory bank to obtain $\{\mathcal{M} \circ \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\}\_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}$, where each $\mathcal{M} \circ \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\in [0,1]^{M\times T'}$ (and $T' = 8$). This is then averaged over the time dimension to obtain $\bar{\mathbf{c}}=[\bar{c}\_1, \bar{c}\_2, \dots, \bar{c}\_M] \in[0, 1]^M$, where $\bar{c}\_i = \frac{2}{NT'} \sum\_{t=1}^{T'}\sum\_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}}{[\mathcal{M} \circ \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})]\_{t,i}}$.

    We then compute the average memory attention for each memory unit $i$ as $\mathbf{C}^i=[\mathbf{c}^i_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}^i_{T'}] \in [0,1]^{M\times T'}$, $c^i\_{t,i} = \bar{c}\_i$ and $c^i\_{t, j} = 0$ for $j\ne i$. This is then fed to decoder $\mathcal{D}$ (using Equation (2)). The decoder outputs are shown in Figure 7(a) in this updated version. As can be seen, they all represent different local patterns.

    To further study how the memory units jointly represent the time series, we feed in the first training sample and obtain the memory attention sequence $\mathbf{C}=[\mathbf{c}\_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}\_{T'}] \in [0,1]^{M\times T'}$ using Equation (1). For each column vector $\mathbf{c}_{t}\in [0, 1]^M$ of $\mathbf{C}$ (i.e. the memory attention), we keep only its top-$k$ values, and set the remaining entries to zero. Let the resultant memory attention matrix be $\mathbf{C}^{(k)}=[\mathbf{c}^{(k)}\_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}^{(k)}\_{T'}]$. Setting $k = 1,2,3,4$, we then feed them into the decoder and obtain the top1, top2, top3, top4 outputs using Equation (2). Results are shown in Figure 7(b) in this updated version. We can observe that i) the top1 curve is around the mean of the time series; ii) the top2 curve has similar shape to the ground truth (i.e., the input time series), which implies that using two memory units can already roughly represent its shape; iii) the top3 and top4 curves are even more refined, providing more details of the time series.

- **Q3. When varying the size of the memory bank - there seems to be no improvement after a given size**

    Yes. This shows that we do not need a large memory. This echos our statement in section 4.2.2 that "when the memory is sufficiently large, further increasing the memory size brings no additional improvement to performance".

- **Q4. Is it possible to determine the memory size analytically somehow, based on the statistics of the dataset?**

    In computer vision, the codebook size (corresponding to the memory size in MATS) is usually empirically set, with a larger codebook for a larger data set [2, 3]. However, to our best knowledge, there is no theoretical studies on the codebook size. Hence, this will be considered as future work.

- **Q5. Seeing the same analysis on other datasets would be useful to answer this question**

    As suggested, we provide additional ablation studies on memory size on the univariate and multivariate versions of Exchange in Appendix A.5. We observe the same trend as in Section 4.2.2, namely that when the memory size is too small, the memory bank cannot store all local patterns, and so the performance is worse. On the other hand, when the memory is sufficiently large, further increasing the memory size brings no additional improvement to performance.

- **Q6. Please add detail on whether you used existing implementations of the competing models shown in Tables 1 & 2, or implemented your own version.**

    For baselines DLinear, DeepTIMe, LSTNet, LSTMa, TCN, and NBeats, we use the implementations from the corresponding authors; for ARIMA, we use the implementation from the Python package `statsmodels2`; for baselines FEDFormer, Autoformer, Informer, Pyraformer, LogTrans, Reformer, LSTM, DLinear, and Repeat-C, we copy their results from the corresponding papers [4, 5, 1]. This is now clarified in Section 4.1 (in blue).

- **Q7. Why did you set $T/T' = 12$ for all datasets? From Table 3 it seems that the best performance comes from $T/T' = 24$.**

    We agree that $T/T' = 24$ performs better on the univariate datasets. However, on multivariate datasets, Table 2 (under Q1) shows that a smaller $T/T'$ ($T/T' = 3$) works better. Hence, as a tradeoff, we set $T/T' = 12$ for all datasets.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer V16Y (2/3)

content.title: Response to Reviewer V16Y (3/3)
content.comment:
- **Q8. The paper is missing details to allow me to really evaluate the transformer vs. LSTM experimental results – e.g. what are the relative sizes of the two architectures (e.g. number of transformer heads, layers, etc.).**

    As suggested by the reviewer, details hyperparameters (heads, layers, etc.) of the transformer used are now added to Appendix A.2 in this revised version.

- **Q9. It is also possible that the complexity of a multivariate dataset would allow the transformer to perform better than the LSTM.**

    As suggested by the reviewer, we add an ablation study on the multivariate versions of the Electricity and Exchange datasets. Results are shown in the Table 3 (Under Q1), and are added (in blue) to Section 4.2.3 in this revised version. As can be seen, LSTM still outperforms Transformer even on the multivariate datasets. While this might be surprising given the usually more powerful performance of the transformer, recently it has been shown that transformers may not be suitable for time series tasks [1].

[1] A. Zeng, M. Chen, L. Zhang, and Q. Xu, "Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?," Preprint arXiv:2205.13504, 2022.

[2] A. Van D., O. Vinyals, et al., "Neural Discrete Representation Learning," in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2017.

[3] P. Esser, R. Rombach, and B. Ommer, "Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis," in Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, 2021.

[4] H. Wu, J. Xu, J. Wang, and M. Long, "Autoformer: Decomposition Transformers with Auto-Correlation for Long-Term Series Forecasting," in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2021.

[5] T. Zhou, Z. Ma, Q. Wen, X. Wang, L. Sun, and R. Jin, "FEDformer: Frequency Enhanced Decomposed Transformer for Long-term Series Forecasting," in International Conference on Machine Learning, 2022.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer V16Y (3/3)

content.title: Nice revision
content.comment:
I thank the authors for their thorough responses and the addition of several experiments. The results of the LSTM vs. Transformer are indeed interesting!

My score is already high, so I will not be changing it. I do think the additional ablation results and results on the multivariate dataset are helpful. In addition, I appreciate the visualizations in the revised Appendix which illustrate the representations that are being learned by the memory units.

I encourage the other reviewers to revisit their evaluations and consider increasing their scores.
